To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
gene expression is a useful endpoint to assess toxicity of pesticides to soil invertebrates and that it is sensitive to very low concentrations of pesticides.
the use of gene expression endpoints in combination with traditional endpoints may be a promising way for pesticide toxicity evaluations.
the effects of the pesticides on gene expression were more pronounced than the effects on the reproduction of springtails.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an alternative approach for the assessment of pesticide effects, which is based on the use of gene expression as a tool to unravel the toxicity of pesticides and their mixtures.
the development and application of ecotoxicological methods to assess the effects of pesticides on non-target terrestrial arthropod communities.
the effects of the commercial products of abametin (Kraft ® 36 EC) and difeno conazole (Score ® 250 EC) on the survival and reproduction of springtails (Folsomia candidata).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
abamectin, difenoconazole and their mixture have the potential to cause adverse effects to the reproduction and gene expression of F. candida.
abamectin, difenoconazole and their mixture have a negative impact on the reproduction of springtail, with the mixture being the most toxic.
the effects of the mixture were not additive, but rather antagonistic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of omic endpoints can provide valuable information on the mode of action of the pesticides, and thus help to understand their toxicological mechanisms.
gene expression endpoints are sensitive and can be useful for the detection of effects in pesticide risk assessments.

the gene expression endpoints used in the present study are sensitive to the effects of pesticides on F. candida, and can be used to evaluate the single toxicity of pesticides and the toxicity of pesticide mixtures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of gene expression as a biomarker of toxicity can be a useful tool in the assessment of the effects of pesticides on non-target soil organisms.
gene expression endpoints can be integrated in traditional bioassay to better evaluate the toxicity of pesticides.
